title: Appendix: Women in the Old Testament
notes: Study aids companion for OT reading

footnotes.text: Examples include Eve (seeMoses 4–5); Sarah (seeGenesis 11–12;16–17); Rebekah (seeGenesis 24); Miriam (seeExodus 15:20–21); Deborah (seeJudges 4–5); Ruth and Naomi (seeRuth 1–4); Hannah (see1 Samuel 1–2); Abigail (see1 Samuel 25); and Esther (seeEsther 1–4). Watson, “Faith and Fortitude: Women of the Old Testament, Part 2,”Ensign, Sept. 2014, 40–45.

For example, seeGenesis 5:2. “The nounʾādāmwithout the definite article, although singular in form, can be a collective or a singular in meaning. When being used as a collective, the word means ‘humanity’ or ‘human beings’ or ‘people’ without regard to gender (e.g.,Gen. 1:26). When used as a singular without the article, the word refers to an individual human being or a person (e.g.,Job 14:1)” (Tremper Longman III and Mark L. Strauss, eds.,The Baker Expository Dictionary of Biblical Words[2023], “Human, Human Being,” 421). For another example, see Michael D. Coogan and others, eds.,The New Oxford Annotated Bible: New Revised Standard Version, 5th ed. (2018), 111, note onExodus 20:1–17.

For example, inRomans 7:1Paul uses an inclusive Greek word meant to refer to all fellow believers (women and men), but the King James Version of the Bible uses the term “brethren” (see Longman and Strauss,The Baker Expository Dictionary, “Brother,” 126). Much of the male-centric language found in the Book of Mormon also may refer to both males and females (see Pyper, “I Say unto You, My Brethren,” 101–5.
In the Doctrine and Covenants, the Lord taught, “What I say unto one I say unto all” (Doctrine and Covenants 61:18, 36;82:5;93:49; see alsoJoseph Smith—Matthew 1:46).
